title: Quickstart Templates — Safe Defaults Review Checklist (v1)
content:
Purpose
Use this checklist during review of all quickstart templates (RAG, agents, RAG+agent) to ensure “production shape” from day one. This is not meant to block iteration, but to prevent common ticket drivers: missing timeouts, unclear 429 behavior, streaming disconnects, noisy logs, unsafe tool patterns, and accidental PII leakage.

How to use
- Reviewer marks each item as: [PASS] [NEEDS FIX] [N/A]
- If [NEEDS FIX], add a short note + link to PR/issue.
- If a template intentionally deviates, document why (tradeoff + mitigation) in the template README.

Scope
Applies to:
- API client usage (Hosted API), including streaming + non-streaming
- HTTP server shape (FastAPI/Express/etc.) and workers (ingestion/indexing)
- Tool calling + retrieval tools
- Telemetry (logs/metrics/traces) and log hygiene
- PII guidance and secrets handling


A) Configuration + environment (baseline production ergonomics)
1) Config layering
- [ ] Config can be set via env vars with sensible defaults for local dev.
- [ ] Clear precedence documented (e.g., defaults < .env < environment < CLI flags).
- [ ] Example .env.example is complete and matches code.
- [ ] No template requires editing source code to run (beyond optional customization).

2) Environment variable contract consistency
- [ ] Standard names used (no one-off names per template/language).
- [ ] Required vs optional env vars explicitly listed.
- [ ] Invalid configs fail fast at startup (clear error message, not a late runtime stack trace).

3) Secrets are treated as secrets
- [ ] API keys/tokens never logged, never printed in “debug” by default.
- [ ] .env is in .gitignore and the README repeats “do not commit .env”.
- [ ] Docs include guidance for key rotation and using secret managers in deployed envs.


B) Timeouts (the #1 default we enforce)
4) Client-side request timeouts
- [ ] Every outbound call to Redwood API has an explicit timeout.
- [ ] Timeouts are configurable per route (or at least per service).
- [ ] Streaming has explicit read/idle timeout behavior (don’t hang forever on broken connections).
- [ ] Ingestion pipelines have separate timeouts from user-facing query paths.

5) Server-side timeouts
- [ ] Server enforces an overall request deadline (or equivalent) and returns a clear error.
- [ ] Long-running endpoints (e.g., ingest) are asynchronous or clearly documented with expected durations.

6) Tool timeouts
- [ ] Each tool invocation is wrapped with a hard timeout.
- [ ] Tool timeouts are stricter than overall agent timeout (avoid cascading overruns).
- [ ] Timeouts include sensible defaults and are documented.

Notes / reviewer check:
- Confirm defaults are not “infinite” and are not “so short everything fails.” The goal is safe and predictable.


C) Retries + backoff + rate limits (supportability focus)
7) Retry policy for Redwood API
- [ ] Retries are enabled for retryable failures only (e.g., transient network, 408/429/5xx as appropriate).
- [ ] No retries on non-idempotent operations unless an idempotency key is used.
- [ ] Retry budget exists (max attempts, max total retry time).
- [ ] Backoff uses jitter.

8) 429 handling
- [ ] 429 behavior is documented in README (what user sees, what system does).
- [ ] If Retry-After is provided, client respects it.
- [ ] Template logs/renders a user-actionable message: “rate limited; consider lowering concurrency / request rate, or use Dedicated capacity.”

9) Streaming resilience
- [ ] Template handles partial streams gracefully (client disconnects, proxy buffering, broken TCP).
- [ ] If reconnect/resume is supported by SDK helper, template uses it; otherwise template clearly documents limitations.
- [ ] No “tight loop reconnect” behavior; backoff applies.

10) Circuit breaker / fail-fast behavior
- [ ] There is a mechanism to avoid hammering dependencies during sustained failure (simple circuit breaker, or at least a retry budget + cooldown).
- [ ] For multi-backend setups (vector DB + LLM), failures degrade in a controlled way (see fallback section).


D) Concurrency + resource bounds (avoid accidental self-DoS)
11) Concurrency limits
- [ ] Server has a configurable concurrency limit for LLM calls / tool calls.
- [ ] Worker ingestion has bounded parallelism (not “unbounded async gather”).

12) Payload/size limits
- [ ] Request bodies have a max size (upload/doc ingestion especially).
- [ ] Chunking defaults are documented and safe (avoid enormous single-chunk prompts).
- [ ] Guardrails exist for “too many documents” / “too large document” cases.

13) Memory safety
- [ ] Streaming responses are not buffered entirely in memory.
- [ ] Large file ingestion uses streaming or chunked processing.


E) Input validation + output validation (reduce prompt + tool injection blast radius)
14) Input validation on API endpoints
- [ ] Validate required fields (non-empty query, tenant ID format if required, etc.).
- [ ] Validate allowed values (model name, route/policy, tool selection) against allow-lists.
- [ ] Normalize/trim inputs; reject obviously malformed content early.

15) Prompt injection awareness
- [ ] RAG templates clearly separate retrieved content from system/developer instructions.
- [ ] Template contains guidance: “Treat retrieved text as untrusted input.”
- [ ] Basic defenses present (e.g., do not execute instructions from retrieved docs, do not pass secrets to model).

16) Structured output validation
- [ ] If using structured outputs (JSON mode / schema), validate outputs strictly.
- [ ] Template handles schema validation failures safely (retry with repair prompt at most once, or fail with clear error).


F) Tool calling safety (agent templates + any retrieval-as-tool)
17) Tool allow-list + explicit tool registry
- [ ] Only an explicit set of tools can be called (deny-by-default).
- [ ] Tool names are stable and documented.
- [ ] Tools have clear input schema and output schema.

18) Tool input validation
- [ ] Validate tool arguments; reject unknown fields.
- [ ] Validate URL/domain if any network tool exists (SSRF prevention).
- [ ] Validate file paths if any file tool exists (path traversal prevention).

19) Tool execution sandboxing (as applicable)
- [ ] No arbitrary shell execution.
- [ ] No direct database writes unless explicitly intended and guarded.
- [ ] If a tool triggers side effects (ticket creation/email), require explicit user confirmation pattern or a “dry run” mode by default.

20) Tool error handling
- [ ] Tool failures are caught and classified; agent receives a safe, minimal error message (not stack traces).
- [ ] Errors do not leak secrets or internal URLs.
- [ ] Tool timeouts and cancellation are handled (avoid zombie requests).


G) Data handling + PII (what we log and what we never log)
21) PII guidance is present and specific
- [ ] README includes a “PII and sensitive data” section.
- [ ] Clear examples: what counts as PII, what should be redacted, what should never be stored.
- [ ] Guidance for regulated environments: refer to Private deployment considerations and audit logging expectations.

22) Logging hygiene (PII + secrets)
- [ ] Default logs do not include raw prompts, retrieved documents, tool payloads, or headers.
- [ ] If the template includes “debug logging,” it is opt-in and clearly labeled as unsafe for production.
- [ ] If request/response samples are logged, they are redacted and truncated.

23) Storage hygiene (RAG)
- [ ] Template clearly states where documents and embeddings are stored (local disk, vector DB).
- [ ] Default dev setup doesn’t persist sensitive data longer than needed (document retention guidance).
- [ ] Ingestion pipeline avoids storing raw documents unless explicitly configured.


H) Telemetry defaults (must align with Console expectations)
24) Correlation IDs
- [ ] Each request gets a request_id; request_id is returned to caller.
- [ ] request_id is propagated to downstream calls (LLM requests, vector DB, tools).
- [ ] tenant/user correlation is supported (tenant_id/user_id fields), with clear cardinality guidance.

25) Tracing (OpenTelemetry)
- [ ] Inbound request creates a root span; trace context propagated on outbound calls.
- [ ] Required span attributes are set (per telemetry contract v1): model, route/policy, request_id, tenant_id (if available), error_class.
- [ ] No high-cardinality attributes (full prompt, full URLs with query params, document text).

26) Metrics
- [ ] Latency metrics: overall + critical sub-steps (retrieval, rerank, generation).
- [ ] Token usage metrics emitted (input/output tokens) where available.
- [ ] Error counters by class (rate_limited, timeout, upstream_5xx, validation_error, tool_error).
- [ ] 429 count metric emitted and easy to dashboard.

27) Logs are structured
- [ ] JSON logs (or equivalent structured logging) enabled by default.
- [ ] Standard fields included: timestamp, severity, service, env, request_id, trace_id/span_id, tenant_id (if present), error_class.
- [ ] Stack traces only for unexpected errors; avoid logging them for expected validation failures.

28) Console deep links (nice-to-have, not required)
- [ ] README includes how to find traces/errors in Redwood Console using request_id.


I) Error taxonomy + user-facing errors (avoid “500 with no clue”)
29) Error mapping is explicit
- [ ] Errors are categorized into a small set of stable error codes/classes.
- [ ] Client-facing error messages are actionable and do not leak internals.

30) Retry vs fail behavior is documented
- [ ] README states what the template retries automatically and what it doesn’t.
- [ ] For timeouts/429, includes “what to do next” guidance (reduce concurrency, Dedicated capacity, increase timeouts, etc.).


J) Fallbacks + graceful degradation (keep app online)
31) Model/route fallback (if used)
- [ ] If using routing/fallback policies, behavior is explicit and observable (metric/log field indicates fallback triggered).
- [ ] Fallback does not silently change output structure (schema compatibility considered).

32) Retrieval fallback
- [ ] If vector DB is unavailable, template fails gracefully with a clear error (or provides a degraded mode if explicitly chosen).


K) Health checks + shutdown (production shape)
33) Health endpoints
- [ ] Liveness and readiness endpoints exist and are documented.
- [ ] Readiness checks include critical dependencies (vector DB connectivity if required).

34) Graceful shutdown
- [ ] Server drains in-flight requests; worker finishes/interrupts safely.
- [ ] SIGTERM handling present in Docker/K8s paths.


L) Dependency + supply chain hygiene (minimum bar)
35) Dependency pinning
- [ ] Dependencies are pinned (or at least bounded) with a clear update mechanism.
- [ ] Lockfiles are committed.

36) Security scanning expectations
- [ ] Repo includes guidance/automation for secret scanning.
- [ ] Template README includes “don’t paste secrets into issues/logs.”


M) Docs check (the last mile)
37) README accuracy
- [ ] Copy/paste quickstart works.
- [ ] All commands match repo structure.
- [ ] “Troubleshooting” covers top failures: invalid API key, 429, timeouts, model/region mismatch, CORS (TS), proxy streaming issues.

38) Deployment notes
- [ ] Docker Compose path is documented.
- [ ] K8s manifest path is documented (if included).
- [ ] Dedicated/Private considerations section exists (networking, egress, secret stores, audit logs).


Reviewer notes (fill in)
- Template:
- Language:
- Reviewer:
- Date:
- Summary of changes requested:
- Blocking issues (if any):


Common pitfalls to watch for (from Support + SRE)
- “No timeout” anywhere → requests hang, workers pile up, users think API is down.
- 429 treated as generic error with no guidance → repeated tickets.
- Streaming behind proxies → disconnects; templates must set expectations + include a workaround.
- Logging full prompts/docs → accidental PII leakage.
- Tool calling without allow-list/timeouts → runaway tool loops and surprise side effects.

Change log
- 2025-12-03: Initial checklist draft (Marcus Lin)
- 2026-01-29: Added streaming resilience and explicit 429 doc requirements; tightened tool safety items; aligned telemetry wording with contract v1 (Naomi Feldman / Sean Gallagher feedback)
